summary: Giraisk Linen Group, Inc. (buyer, the firm's client) bought all of the stock of Lakemont Textile Care, Inc. from Pinaix Service Holdings, LLC for $48,500,000. Lakemont is a New York commercial laundry and linen-rental business with plants in Yonkers, NY and Newark, NJ, and healthcare customers provide most of its revenue. The Stock Purchase Agreement was signed March 2, 2026 and the deal closed April 15, 2026. The folder holds: the SPA; a post-closing side letter dated October 26, 2026, which extends the deadline to replace Seller's credit support and records a dispute over an escrow claim notice; the Escrow Agreement with Fernhill Trust Company, N.A.; the Key Employee Agreement of Lakemont's President; a Bill of Sale for tunnel-washer equipment from a Seller affiliate; the Disclosure Schedule; and an IP Assignment Agreement for the LinenLoop RFID tracking software. It also holds two distractors: a February 2026 prior draft of the SPA and the 2025 mutual NDA. Five issues are planted. (1) The Escrow Agreement chooses Delaware law and an exclusive Delaware forum for escrow disputes, while the SPA chooses New York law and an exclusive New York forum. (2) The side letter folds Buyer's credit-support indemnity into an SPA covenant indemnity that the SPA leaves outside the cap. (3) Buyer's escrow claim notice was delivered after the Initial Release Date computed from the Closing Date. (4) The Pre-Closing Tax indemnity in the SPA survives only as long as the 12-month general tax representation. (5) The Key Employee Agreement defines 'Business' to exclude the healthcare linen services at the core of the SPA's definition, so the President's non-compete does not reach them.

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: Escrow Agreement Section 8.2 provides that the Escrow Agreement is governed by the laws of the State of Delaware. It also requires that any dispute arising out of or relating to the Escrow Agreement or the Escrow Funds, including entitlement to any release, be brought exclusively in the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware. SPA Sections 11.9 and 11.10 choose New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of New York County courts for any action arising out of the SPA or any Transaction Document. Each clause is ordinary on its own. Read together, Buyer's indemnity claims must be litigated in New York, while the fight over releasing the $4,850,000 escrow (Buyer's main source of recovery) belongs in Delaware under Delaware law. That creates two conflicting exclusive-forum clauses and a risk of parallel proceedings and inconsistent rulings. The SPA's precedence clause (Section 11.4) does not cure the conflict. It ranks the SPA only over the Disclosure Schedule, Bill of Sale and IP Assignment Agreement, and does not mention the Escrow Agreement. The Escrow Agreement was also signed later, on April 15, 2026, and binds the Escrow Agent, who is not a party to the SPA.
detect_terms: laws of the State of Delaware
Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware
issues.expected_finding: The Escrow Agreement's Delaware governing law and exclusive Delaware Chancery forum conflict with the SPA's New York law and exclusive New York forum, and the SPA's precedence clause does not reach the Escrow Agreement, so Buyer faces split proceedings over its indemnity claims and the escrow; the clauses should be conformed to New York law and forum by amendment signed by all three parties.
detect_terms2: laws of the State of New York

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: SPA Section 9.5(c) states that the Cap and Deductible apply only to claims under Section 9.2(a) and Section 9.3(a), the representation-and-warranty indemnities. Covenant indemnities under Sections 9.2(b) and 9.3(b) are therefore uncapped for both sides, which looks balanced. Side Letter Section 3 (dated October 26, 2026) extends Buyer's deadline to replace Seller's Retained Credit Support. That support consists of Seller's guaranty of the Company's Yonkers plant lease, which runs through June 30, 2034 at about $1,150,000 per year, and a $3,000,000 performance bond under the Saint Odile Health System contract. In return, Buyer agrees to indemnify Seller for all Losses under the Retained Credit Support, and that indemnity is 'deemed an obligation of Buyer under Section 9.3(b)' of the SPA. On its own, this appears to bring the indemnity within the SPA's negotiated framework. Read together with Section 9.5(c), it makes Buyer's parent-level indemnity for the lease and bond completely uncapped. No other limit in Article IX applies to Section 9.3(b) claims.
detect_terms: shall apply only to claims under Section 9.2(a) and Section 9.3(a)
issues.expected_finding: Because the side letter makes Buyer's credit-support indemnity a Section 9.3(b) obligation and SPA Section 9.5(c) applies the Cap only to Sections 9.2(a) and 9.3(a), Buyer has unlimited parent-level liability for the Yonkers lease guaranty and the $3,000,000 performance bond; the side letter should impose a specific dollar cap and time limit on that indemnity.
detect_terms2: deemed an obligation of Buyer under Section 9.3(b)

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: Escrow Agreement Section 4.2 sets the Initial Release Date at 180 days after the Closing Date. On that date, the Escrow Agent releases 50% of the Escrow Amount ($2,425,000), less only amounts covered by Claim Notices delivered before the Initial Release Date. The Escrow Agreement recitals state the Closing Date as April 15, 2026, so the Initial Release Date was October 12, 2026. Side Letter Section 5 (dated October 26, 2026) records that Buyer delivered a Claim Notice dated October 19, 2026 for $1,300,000 of Saint Odile Health System overbilling credits. It also records that Seller has demanded release of the Initial Release Amount, and that Buyer disputes the release and reserves its position that the claim must be withheld. That notice came seven days after the window closed. Buyer has not agreed to the release, so the point is still live.
issues.expected_finding: Buyer's October 19, 2026 Claim Notice was delivered after the October 12, 2026 Initial Release Date (180 days after the April 15, 2026 Closing Date), so Seller is entitled to release of $2,425,000 regardless of the $1,300,000 claim; Buyer should negotiate a holdback from that amount and preserve a direct claim against Seller under SPA Article IX before the general survival period ends on April 15, 2027.

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: SPA Section 9.2(c) has Seller indemnify Buyer for Pre-Closing Taxes. Section 9.1(c) provides that this indemnity survives only until the end of the survival period applicable to the representations in Section 4.16 (Taxes). Section 9.1(a) and (b) treat Section 4.16 as a general representation, not a Fundamental Representation, so it survives only 12 months after the Closing Date. The Pre-Closing Tax indemnity therefore lapses on April 15, 2027. Assessment periods for the Company's 2024 and 2025 New York, New Jersey and federal returns stay open for years after that. The Disclosure Schedule (Schedule 4.16) also discloses an open New York sales and use tax audit for 2023 and 2024. As a result, most pre-closing tax exposure will surface only after Buyer's indemnity rights have expired. Nothing in the Disclosure Schedule or any other document extends this period.
detect_terms: survival period applicable to the representations in Section 4.16
issues.expected_finding: Because Section 9.1(c) ties the Pre-Closing Tax indemnity to the 12-month survival of the Section 4.16 tax representation, Buyer loses tax indemnity protection on April 15, 2027, well before the applicable assessment periods close; the indemnity should survive until 60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations.

issues.label: defined term inconsistency
issues.description: Key Employee Agreement Section 1 defines 'Business' independently as commercial laundry and linen services provided to hotels, resorts and restaurants. Section 7 uses that defined term for the President's non-competition and customer non-solicitation covenants. SPA Section 1.1 defines 'Business' as commercial laundry, linen rental and textile processing services for healthcare, hospitality and industrial customers. The Disclosure Schedule shows healthcare customers, led by Saint Odile Health System, provide most of the Company's revenue. Read against the SPA definition, the Key Employee Agreement leaves the Company's President free to compete for, and solicit, the healthcare accounts that are the core of what Buyer purchased. The SPA's precedence clause does not reach the Key Employee Agreement, and the Key Employee Agreement does not incorporate the SPA definition.
issues.expected_finding: The Key Employee Agreement's definition of 'Business' omits the healthcare and industrial linen services included in the SPA definition, so the President's non-compete and non-solicit do not protect the Company's principal healthcare revenue; the definition should be amended to match SPA Section 1.1.
